I'm a 68-year-old farmer in Quzhou County, and I've been working this land for 51 years. That's longer than most people in our village have been alive. I started farming at 17, and over the decades I've seen good years and bad years, droughts and floods, high prices and prices so low they weren't worth the diesel to haul the grain to market. My education—agricultural college back in the 1970s—gave me a framework for thinking systematically, but it's the 51 years of watching crops grow on *my* fields that I trust most.

This year I'm managing 30.4 mu. Twenty-four mu goes to the wheat-maize double crop, which is the backbone of our farm. The other 6.4 mu I keep in millet—for family consumption, for some local sale, and because millet doesn't need the intensive irrigation and fertilizer that wheat and maize demand. At my age, I have to be realistic about labor. My wife and I do what we can, and my youngest son is still around to help with the heavy work, but two of my children work off-farm in Handan and only come back for harvest. So I hire labor for planting and harvest on the wheat-maize fields. It's an expense, but at 68, my back tells me it's necessary.

**Winter wheat (24 mu):** The maize came off these fields last week, and the stubble is still fresh. I ran the rotary tiller yesterday to chop the residue and open the soil. I'll plant around October 8-10 if the weather holds—I've learned not to plant too early or the wheat gets too tall before winter and freezes. I'm using an improved Jimai variety, not the newest hybrid but one I know performs well on my soil. For fertilizer, I'm targeting about 20 kg N per mu total: 50 kg of compound fertilizer (15-15-15) as base before planting, and I'll topdress with 20 kg of urea at jointing in March if the wheat looks strong. That's about 8 kg P₂O₅ and 5 kg K₂O per mu. I'll irrigate three times—jointing, heading, and grain filling—groundwater pumping is expensive at nearly 40 yuan per mu per irrigation, but wheat pays back if you don't cut corners. I'm expecting around 480 kg/mu if the spring cooperates.

**Summer maize (24 mu):** This gets planted immediately after wheat harvest in early June, sometimes within 48 hours. The window is brutal. I use a hybrid—Zhengdan series or similar—with a yield potential over 500 kg/mu. I band fertilizer at planting: about 40 kg compound per mu, then topdress urea at the 6-8 leaf stage. Total N around 18 kg/mu, P around 6 kg/mu, K around 4 kg/mu. Maize in summer usually gets two irrigations, but if July rains are good I might skip one and save the pumping cost. I always spray herbicide at planting and watch for corn borer—if I see moths in June, I'll add insecticide.

**Millet (6.4 mu):** This land is separate, and I just finished the millet harvest here last week. Next spring, around mid-May when the soil warms, I'll plant a local drought-tolerant variety. Millet is forgiving. I apply one base dressing of compound fertilizer—about 30 kg/mu, giving roughly 12 kg N, 5 kg P, 3 kg K—and irrigate once or twice depending on the monsoon. Yield should be around 280 kg/mu, enough for family porridge through the winter and some sales at the village market.

The big constraint this year is cash flow. With three children working off-farm, the household income is stable, but I still keep a reserve. I'm not cutting fertilizer below what the crops need—that's false economy—but I'm also not chasing record yields with extra inputs that might not pay back. At 68, I've learned that consistent, moderate management beats gambling on the weather.
